paragraphs.heading: What a trajectory is
paragraphs.text: A trajectory is the path an object follows as it moves over time. The object might be a projectile or a satellite, or a planet, asteroid or comet travelling around a central mass. In classical mechanics, Hamiltonian mechanics defines a complete trajectory by position and momentum together. The word is used outside physics too: control theory uses it for a set of states of a dynamical system, listed in time order.

paragraphs.heading: A thrown stone
paragraphs.text: One familiar trajectory is the path of a thrown ball or rock. In a much simplified model, only a uniform pull of gravity acts on it, and the path comes out as a parabola. That is a good approximation for a rock tossed a short way on the Moon. In general, though, working out a trajectory may mean allowing for gravity that varies and for air resistance, and that is the job of ballistics.

paragraphs.heading: Galileo's idealised path
paragraphs.text: Galileo Galilei first studied the ideal case of a projectile in uniform gravity with no other forces such as air drag. Throughout the Middle Ages in Europe, practical investigators would have seen ignoring the air as a pointless idea. Galileo expected a vacuum to exist, which his collaborator Evangelista Torricelli later showed on Earth, and this let him start the future science of mechanics. In a near vacuum, such as on the Moon, his simple parabola turns out to be essentially right.

paragraphs.heading: Orbits
paragraphs.text: A major success of Newtonian mechanics was deriving Kepler's laws of planetary motion. Around a point mass, or a spherically symmetrical mass such as the Sun, a moving object follows a conic section, usually an ellipse or a hyperbola. This matches the orbits of planets, comets and spacecraft reasonably well. A comet that passes close to the Sun is also pushed by the solar wind and radiation pressure, which alter its orbit and make it throw material into space.

paragraphs.heading: How far and how high
paragraphs.text: Let g be the acceleration of gravity, and launch a projectile from flat ground at speed v and angle θ. Its starting horizontal speed is vₕ = vcos (θ) and its starting vertical speed is v_v = vsin (θ). The range is 2v_hv_v/g and the highest point reached is v_v²/2g. For a given launch speed, the range is greatest when vₕ = v_v, which means a launch angle of 45 degrees, and that range is v²/g.

paragraphs.heading: The law underneath
paragraphs.text: Picture a particle of mass m travelling through a potential field V. The mass stands for inertia, and V stands for a kind of outside force called conservative. If you know V at every point that matters, you can work out the force acting at each point, such as the force from gravity, though not every force can be described this way. The equation of the trajectory is then Newton's second law: force equals mass times acceleration.
